content: Allergic Reactions: Dicloxacillin can cause allergic reactions, which may manifest as red bumps on the skin (hives), nausea, vomiting, dizziness, lightheadedness, fainting, stomach cramps, or joint pain. If you experience any of these symptoms, stop taking the medication and seek medical attention immediately. Antibiotic-Associated Diarrhea: Dicloxacillin, like many antibiotics, can lead to an overgrowth of Clostridioides difficile (C. diff) in the gut, resulting in antibiotic-associated diarrhea. This condition can occur even up to two months after stopping the medication. Symptoms include watery diarrhea, persistent diarrhea, blood in the stool, severe stomach cramps, and fever. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience any of these symptoms. Seizures: Some individuals taking dicloxacillin have reported seizures. Seizures can present in various ways, including muscle twitching, jerking, spasms, tremors, or other uncontrolled movements; stiffening of the arms and legs; feelings of anxiety, nervousness, confusion, or dread; dizziness or lightheadedness; and loss of consciousness or falling. If you experience any of these signs, stop taking dicloxacillin and contact your healthcare provider immediately. Kidney Damage: Dicloxacillin may cause kidney damage. Symptoms of kidney damage include reduced urination, swelling in the feet, ankles, or legs, unusual weakness or fatigue, difficulty breathing, chest pain or pressure, confusion, nausea, or seizures. If you notice any of these symptoms, contact your healthcare provider immediately. Blood Disorders: Dicloxacillin can lead to blood disorders such as eosinophilia, hemolytic anemia, agranulocytosis, neutropenia, leukopenia, or bone marrow depression. Symptoms of blood disorders include fever, shortness of breath, pale or yellowish skin, easy bruising or bleeding, frequent infections, unusual weakness or fatigue, dizziness, lightheadedness, fainting, headache, or an abnormal or fast heartbeat. Stop taking dicloxacillin and seek medical attention immediately if you experience any of these symptoms. Liver Damage: Dicloxacillin can cause liver damage, also known as hepatotoxicity. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, stomach or abdominal pain, fever, unusual weakness or fatigue, itching, loss of appetite, light-colored stools, dark-colored urine, or yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice). Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you experience any of these symptoms. Precautions: Who Should Not Use Dicloxacillin? Do not take dicloxacillin if you are allergic to it or any of its ingredients. Your pharmacist can provide a list of ingredients in the specific product you are prescribed. How to Take Dicloxacillin: Take dicloxacillin on an empty stomach with a large glass of water (at least 4 ounces or 120 milliliters) at least one hour before or two hours after a meal. Remain sitting or standing upright while taking dicloxacillin. Avoid taking it while lying down or just before going to bed. Only take dicloxacillin if it has been prescribed to you by a healthcare provider. Do not share this medication with others, even if they have the same condition, as it may harm them. Keep dicloxacillin out of reach of children. What to Tell Your Healthcare Provider: Inform your healthcare provider about all your health conditions and any prescription or over-the-counter (OTC) medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, or supplements you are using. This will help them determine if dicloxacillin is appropriate for you. Specifically, mention if you have a history of penicillin allergy, asthma, gastrointestinal issues (e.g., nausea, vomiting, or antibiotic-associated diarrhea), kidney problems, or if you are pregnant or breastfeeding. Drug Interactions: Dicloxacillin may interact with other medications and supplements. Always inform your healthcare provider about any prescription or OTC medications, vitamins, minerals, herbal products, or supplements you are taking. Avoid taking additional medications, including OTC products like antacids, laxatives, or vitamins, without consulting your physician. Specific medications to discuss with your healthcare provider include: Tetracyclines (e.g., tetracycline, doxycycline, minocycline, omadacycline, sarecycline) Probenecid (commonly used for gout) Warfarin (a blood thinner) This may not be a complete list of potential interactions, so consult your healthcare provider for more details. Overdose: If you or someone else has taken too much dicloxacillin, seek medical help immediately. Call 911 or contact a Poison Control Center at 800-222-1222. Missed Dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and take only the next scheduled dose. Do not take double or extra doses. Complete the full prescribed course of dicloxacillin, even if your symptoms improve, to reduce the risk of antibiotic resistance. Side Effects: Common Side Effects: Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and a black hairy tongue are the most common side effects. Inform your healthcare provider if these symptoms bother you. Serious Side Effects: Severe allergic reactions, antibiotic-associated diarrhea, seizures, kidney damage, blood disorders, and liver damage are less common but serious side effects. If you experience any of these, stop taking dicloxacillin and seek medical attention immediately.
